items.title: 1.5% to 5.0%: The Atlanta Fed's Tracker Signals a Growth Rebound, So Why Does the Economy Still Feel So Weak?
items.body:
Two very different pictures of the U.S. economy are circulating at the same time. In one, a widely watched Atlanta Fed estimate points to third-quarter growth near 5.0%, a sharp step up from 1.5% in the second quarter. In the other, households report low confidence and inflation remains stubborn, with the July reading on the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index at 3.7%.

Both can be true. Understanding why starts with what the growth number actually measures, what is driving it, and what it leaves out.

## What the GDPNow Tracker Is (and Isn't)

GDPNow is a running estimate published by the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta. It takes incoming economic data, such as retail sales, manufacturing, housing, trade, and inventories, and translates it into a real-time estimate of what quarterly GDP growth might look like once the official figures are released.

A few points are worth keeping in mind:

- **It is a model, not an official statistic.** The government's official GDP numbers come from the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA). GDPNow is not a forecast from Federal Reserve policymakers.
- **It moves.** Each new data release can shift the estimate, sometimes significantly, especially when a quarter is not yet complete.
- **It can miss.** Nowcasts have at times landed well above or below the first official reading, so a headline near 5.0% is best read as a signal of momentum rather than a final answer.

## The Numbers Behind the Rebound

The estimate for the third quarter is driven largely by two components:

| Component | Reported figure | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Overall real GDP growth (Q3 tracking estimate) | Near 5.0% | Up from 1.5% in Q2 |
| Private investment | Up 18.7% | Business spending on equipment, software, structures, and inventories can swing sharply from quarter to quarter |
| Consumer spending | Up 4.2% | Household spending makes up roughly two-thirds of the economy, so even modest changes carry weight |

Growth rates for a single quarter are conventionally quoted at an annualized pace, which is why the figures can look larger than everyday intuition suggests. A jump in investment of this size also tends to be concentrated in a few categories rather than spread evenly across the economy.

## Why It Still Feels Weak

If output is accelerating, why does sentiment sag? Economists point to several overlapping explanations.

**1. Prices are still the main complaint.** Growth statistics are adjusted for inflation, but household budgets are not experienced as a rate of change. They are experienced as a level. Even if inflation cools, groceries, rent, insurance, and utilities cost more than they did a few years ago. With the July PCE reading at 3.7%, prices are still rising faster than many households would like, and that shapes how people feel about their finances regardless of what GDP shows.

**2. Sentiment surveys measure mood, not just money.** Consumer confidence gauges reflect perceptions about prices, interest rates, job security, and the news cycle. Historically, what people say in surveys and what they actually spend have not always moved together. It is possible for people to feel pessimistic and still keep spending.

**3. Aggregate spending can hide uneven experiences.** A 4.2% rise in consumer spending is an average across all households. Research on consumption patterns has often found that a large share of total spending comes from higher-income households, while lower- and middle-income families may feel more pressure from everyday costs.

**4. An investment boom is not the same as a paycheck boom.** Spending on buildings, equipment, and technology adds to GDP right away. But it does not automatically translate into higher wages, lower borrowing costs, or cheaper essentials for the average household.

## The AI Data-Center Question

The most debated part of the story is how much of the investment surge is tied to the buildout of artificial-intelligence infrastructure: data-center construction, servers and chips, networking gear, and the power and cooling systems that support them. These outlays are counted as business investment, and when they accelerate, they can lift the headline growth figure noticeably.

That raises a few questions economists are weighing:

- **How much is imported?** Much of the advanced hardware is produced abroad. In GDP accounting, imports are subtracted, so a surge in spending on imported equipment does not add as much to domestic output as the investment figure alone might suggest.
- **How concentrated is it?** If a relatively small number of large companies account for a large share of the spending, changes in their plans could reverse the contribution quickly.
- **How durable is it?** Investment is inherently lumpy. A strong quarter does not guarantee the next one, and the payoff from these projects, in productivity and profits, will take time to become clear.
- **What does it do for everyone else?** Construction, electrical work, and energy demand may benefit locally, but the broader effect on jobs and household income is harder to measure and still being studied.

None of this means the expansion is fragile or that the spending is misplaced. It means the composition of growth matters as much as the headline.

## What to Watch on Sept. 30

Two data releases due on Sept. 30 could sharpen the picture:

1. **The revision to second-quarter GDP.** The 1.5% figure for Q2 is the base against which the third-quarter rebound is being measured. A revision up or down would change how large the swing looks.
2. **August PCE inflation.** The PCE index is the inflation gauge the Federal Reserve tracks most closely. Whether the July pace of 3.7% eases, holds, or picks up will matter for household sentiment and for expectations about interest rates. It is also worth checking whether a given figure is the headline or the "core" measure (which excludes food and energy), and whether it is a monthly or annual change, since they can tell different stories.

The first official estimate of third-quarter GDP will come only after the quarter ends, so the tracker's number will continue to shift as new data arrive.

## The Bottom Line

A strong growth estimate and a gloomy public mood are not necessarily a contradiction. GDP measures the total value of what the economy produces, while sentiment reflects how people experience prices, borrowing costs, and job prospects in daily life. When growth leans on business investment, particularly in a single fast-moving area such as AI infrastructure, the gap between the statistics and the lived experience can widen.

For readers trying to make sense of the data, a few habits help: look at several indicators rather than one, distinguish between estimates and official releases, and pay attention to what is driving a number rather than only how large it is.

*This article is for general information only and is not financial, investment, or economic advice. Figures cited reflect the Atlanta Fed's GDPNow tracker and related government data as reported at the time of writing and may be revised in later releases.*

items.title: $810 Million and a Ticking Clock: Why the White House's Pocket Rescission Has Even Sen. Susan Collins Objecting
items.body:
With days left in the federal fiscal year, the White House has asked to cancel $810 million that Congress already approved. The request uses a rarely seen budget tool called a **pocket rescission**, and it has drawn objections from the Republican who chairs the Senate Appropriations Committee.

Below is a plain-language summary of what was announced, why the timing matters, and what happens next.

## What the White House is asking for

According to reporting from CNBC, CNN, ABC News and others, the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) sent Congress a package on Friday, Sept. 25. It seeks to cancel about $810 million in previously approved spending.

The largest piece is roughly **$567 million** in funding for programs run through the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). Reporting ties it to the Refugee and Entrant Assistance account, which supports the Office of Refugee Resettlement and services for refugees, asylees and other non-citizens. The package also reportedly includes about $28 million for HHS research. It includes smaller items elsewhere in the government, such as $15 million for a Department of Homeland Security case-management pilot for people under immigration supervision who are not detained.

The administration says these programs are unnecessary. Its description of the HHS money refers to "pro-illegal immigration programs" and outside organizations that serve non-citizens. Officials have also argued that the refugee office is overfunded now that border crossings have fallen.

## What a pocket rescission is, and why the timing matters

Under the Impoundment Control Act of 1974, a president can ask Congress to cancel, or "rescind," money it has appropriated. Once the request is sent, the funds can be withheld for up to 45 days of continuous session. During that time Congress can pass a bill approving the cancellation. If it doesn't, the money is supposed to be released.

A **pocket rescission** is a request sent so late in the fiscal year that the 45-day window runs past Sept. 30. The money expires before Congress is required to vote on the request. In effect, the funds run out while the request is still pending.

Critics say the timing is the whole point. This year the request arrived five days before the fiscal year ended. The House is also out of session until after the November elections, so lawmakers have almost no chance to respond.

## Why Collins and the GAO say it breaks the law

The Government Accountability Office (GAO), Congress's nonpartisan watchdog, has concluded that pocket rescissions are not allowed under the Impoundment Control Act. It reasons that a request timed so Congress cannot act on it lets the president bypass Congress's authority over federal spending.

Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who chairs the Senate Appropriations Committee, cited that finding in her criticism. In a statement, she called any attempt to rescind appropriated funds without congressional approval "a clear violation of the law." She also said OMB "intentionally withheld these funds for months" to carry out the cancellation. She noted that Congress approved the money on a bipartisan basis and that it was signed into law.

Democrats have been sharper. Rep. Brendan Boyle of Pennsylvania, the top Democrat on the House Budget Committee, said the administration knows it cannot get these cuts through Congress and is making them "through the back door." Sen. Jeff Merkley of Oregon called the tactic "an illegal line item veto" and urged Republicans to imagine a Democratic president doing the same.

## Not the first time

The tactic is not new to this administration. Last year it sent a pocket rescission of about $4.9 billion in foreign aid near the end of the fiscal year. GAO called that move unlawful as well. The dispute went to the courts, and the Supreme Court, acting on an emergency request, allowed much of that money to expire without settling the underlying legal question.

That history explains why both sides are watching this round closely. The administration has defended pocket rescissions as a legitimate use of its budget authority. Critics say the earlier outcome encouraged its use again.

## Who is affected

If the cancellation stands, the effect will be felt by the groups that receive federal money for refugee and non-citizen services. That includes resettlement agencies, community organizations and the local programs that depend on them. The cuts also reach some research and immigration-related programs. The exact effect on any one program will depend on how much of its money has already been spent or committed, and that is not clear from public reporting.

## What to watch next

- **Whether the money is released or lapses.** Under the administration's approach, the funds expire on Sept. 30 unless a court or Congress intervenes.
- **Legal challenges.** Affected organizations or members of Congress could go to court, as happened after the 2025 rescission.
- **Congressional response.** Collins's objection is notable because it comes from the party that controls Congress and from the chair who oversees the spending bills. It could shape how future appropriations are written.
- **Guardrails in future funding bills.** Lawmakers in both parties may push for language that limits or bans late-year rescission requests.

## The bottom line

This dispute is about more than one $810 million package. It is about who has the final say over federal spending. The Constitution gives Congress the power of the purse. The administration argues it has the flexibility to stop spending it considers wasteful. Critics, including a senior Republican appropriator and GAO, say the pocket rescission is a way around the process that Congress wrote into law.

*This article is a summary of public reporting as of Sept. 27, 2026, and details may change as the situation develops. It is for general information only and is not legal or financial advice.*

**Sources and further reading:**
- [CNBC: White House moves to block $810 million in funding through pocket rescission](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/26/white-house-810-million-pocket-rescission.html)
- [CNN: Trump admin cancels funding for refugees, immigrant detainees and others](https://www.cnn.com/2026/09/26/politics/trump-administrion-pocket-rescissions)
- [ABC News: White House orders over $800M in funds rescinded; Collins calls it 'clear violation' of law](https://abcnews.com/Politics/white-house-orders-800m-funds-rescinded-collins-calls/story?id=136772703)
- [TIME: What Is a 'Pocket Rescission'?](https://time.com/article/2026/09/26/what-is-a-pocket-rescission-inside-trump-s-move-to-cancel-810-million-in-federal-funding/)

items.title: 6-3 and a Citizenship Database: Why the Supreme Court Let the SAVE System Keep Checking Voter Rolls Weeks Before the Midterms
items.body:
On September 25, 2026, the Supreme Court granted an emergency request from the Justice Department and paused a lower-court order that had blocked the administration's overhauled SAVE system. The vote was 6-3. With Election Day on November 3, less than six weeks away, the order lets federal agencies keep sharing citizenship data with state and local election officials who want to verify their voter lists.

The order is temporary and does not end the case. Even so, it settles for now a question that has drawn attention from election officials, privacy advocates, and voting-rights groups: how far the federal government can go in helping states check who is a citizen.

## What SAVE Is and What Changed

SAVE stands for Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements. It is a federal data system that dates back to the 1980s. Government agencies originally used it to confirm the immigration status of people applying for public benefits or licenses.

According to news reports, the Department of Homeland Security overhauled the system in 2025. The changes:

- **Broader data.** SAVE was linked for the first time with Social Security Administration records, which cover most Americans and not only noncitizens.
- **Bulk searches.** States and localities can upload entire voter lists instead of checking one person at a time.
- **A new use.** Election officials can run registered voters through the system to look for possible noncitizens.

NPR reported that 26 states had uploaded voter data and that the system had checked more than 65 million voters. About 28,635 were flagged as potential noncitizens. A flag is not a finding. It is a lead that officials are expected to follow up, and in Texas, roughly one in five of 2,724 flagged voters was later confirmed to be a citizen and reinstated, according to the same reporting. The government has not publicly released an overall error rate.

## How the Case Got to the Supreme Court

The League of Women Voters, the Electronic Privacy Information Center, and five individuals sued the Department of Homeland Security, the Social Security Administration, and the Department of Justice. They argued that combining and sharing sensitive personal records this way broke federal law.

In June 2026, U.S. District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan agreed. She found that the aggregation and disclosure of the data violated the Social Security Act, the Privacy Act, and the Administrative Procedure Act. She wrote that the government had "knowingly trampled on the privacy rights of American citizens in a manner that threatens the sacred right to vote," and she blocked the revised system.

The administration asked the Supreme Court to stay that order while the case continued.

## Why the Majority Let SAVE Continue

The Court's unsigned order said the voting-rights groups' claims about the legality of the modified system "likely lack merit," and that the Court was likely to reverse the district court's ruling. It also said the federal government "has an obligation to respond to requests from state and local election officials seeking to verify the citizenship of voters."

Reporting on the order highlights two more points:

1. **Individualized checks.** The majority stressed the use of SAVE to check individual voters' citizenship as the election approaches.
2. **The 90-day rule.** Federal law generally bars systematic programs to remove voters from the rolls within 90 days of a federal election. That window is already open for the midterms. Reporters noted that this limits how the tool can be used before November.

In short, the majority signaled that officials may verify specific voters but should not run large-scale purges this close to the election.

## Jackson's Dissent

Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan, and Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented. Jackson wrote the dissent. She faulted the majority for not weighing the harms that could follow if the modified system keeps operating. One risk she named was that states might cancel the registrations of at least some recently naturalized citizens, or make them show proof of citizenship before voting.

Her central argument was about how to weigh the two sides:

> "[T]he harm caused by burdening or disenfranchising even a few lawful voters outweighs the nonexistent harm that the Government experiences when it is prevented from taking an action that it likely lacks the authority to take."

Coverage of the dissent also noted her objection that the Court acted on its emergency docket without full briefing or oral argument.

## The Two Sides in Plain Terms

**Supporters of the decision** say election officials need reliable tools to keep voter rolls accurate. They say the federal government holds data states cannot easily get elsewhere, and that Congress and the Court have treated accurate rolls as a legitimate goal. Noncitizen voting is illegal under federal law, and supporters argue that verification protects public confidence in elections.

**Critics** say the system can wrongly flag eligible voters. Naturalized citizens, whose records may not match every federal database, are the group most often cited. They also worry about privacy when Social Security data is used for a purpose it was not built for, and about mistakes that come too late for a voter to fix before Election Day.

Both concerns are recognized in the order itself. The majority points to the 90-day limit and to individualized review. The dissent points to the risk that errors reach real voters.

## What Happens Next

- **The case continues.** A stay pauses the lower court's order but is not a final ruling on the merits. The litigation over the system's legality goes on.
- **State practices will vary.** Each state decides whether and how to use SAVE and what follow-up process applies to flagged voters.
- **Timing matters.** With less than six weeks to Election Day, any verification step that leads to a registration problem leaves little time to correct it.

## What Voters Can Do

Nothing in the order changes who is eligible to vote or the basic rules for casting a ballot. A few practical steps are worth taking whatever your view of the ruling:

- **Check your registration** on your state or local election office's official website.
- **Respond promptly** if you receive a notice asking you to confirm your eligibility or citizenship. Keep any documents the notice asks for.
- **Contact your local election office** if you believe your record is wrong. It can explain the correction process and deadlines.
- **Confirm key dates** for registration, early voting, and mail ballots with official state sources.

## The Bottom Line

The Supreme Court's 6-3 order keeps a revised federal citizenship-verification system running during the final weeks before the midterms. The majority views the legal challenge as unlikely to succeed and stresses individualized checks. The dissenters warn that even a small number of wrongly burdened voters is too high a cost. The case is not over. In the meantime, voters and election officials will work under the order's limits, including the 90-day rule on systematic removals.

*This article is a news summary for general information and is not legal advice. Details are based on published reporting as of September 2026 and may change as the case develops. For official guidance on your voter registration, contact your state or local election office.*

**Reporting referenced:** [NPR](https://www.npr.org/2026/09/25/nx-s1-5976804/supreme-court-trump-save-noncitizen-voting), [CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/supreme-court-trump-save-database-voter-citizenship/), [CNN](https://www.cnn.com/2026/09/25/politics/supreme-court-voter-roll-non-citizen-save), [NBC News](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/supreme-court/supreme-court-allows-trump-administration-use-expanded-database-potent-rcna596611)
